It should be noted that the concept of resonance does not mean that these structures rapidly shifts between canonical forms. In fact, all the molecules of a substance have the same structure all the time, in which all the electrons are delocalized over the whole system involved in resonance.

Resonance Energy and Stability of Benzene

The resonance energy of a molecules is the difference between the energy of the most stable canonical form and that of the actual molecule. For benzene it can be calculated by measuring its heat of hydrogenation and comparing it with that of the most stable canonical from.

Hydrogenation of cyclohexene (having one double bond) evolves 120 kJ/mol heat energy to form cyclohexane.

Hydrogenation of cyclohexa–1,3–diene (having two double bonds) evolves 232 kJ/mol to form cyclohexane, which is almost double of the value 120 kJ/mol for cyclohexene.

The molecule cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene (Kekule structure) normally written for benzene and having three double bonds, should release energy three time to that of cyclohexane (i.e. 120×3 = 360 kJ/mol), upon hydrogenation.

But hydrogenation of benzene actually evolves only 208 kJ/mol.

Thus, the measured (experimental) heat of hydrogenation of benzene is less than the expected value of the most stable canonical form by an amount of 152 kJ/mol. Benzene is, therefore, is said to be resonance stabilized by an amount of 152 kJ/mol which is known as its resonance energy.

16.8.5 Reactivity and Reactions

Due to unusual stability (resonance stabilization), benzene and its derivatives do not give addition reactions like those of alkenes. In alkenes the pi electronic cloud is localized between the two carbon atoms and thus they readily undergo addition reactions. In benzene the pi electronic cloud makes a continuous sheet above and below all the six nuclei and the pi electrons are, thus delocalized, which give benzene more stability. Benzene, therefore, prefers to undergo electrophilic substitution reactions rather than addition reactions, to retain its aromatic character.

16.8.5.1 Addition Reactions

Benzene is very resistant to addition reaction and requires much more vigorous conditions than generally required for alkenes and alkynes. It does not undergo electrophilic addition reaction, but may give free-radical type addition and catalytic addition reactions in proper conditions.

16.8.5.1.1 Addition of Hydrogen

Benzene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of Ni, Pt or Pd catalyst at elevated temperature and high pressure to form cyclohexane. The reaction is also called catalytic hydrogenation.

Similarly toluene (a benzene derivative) upon catalytic hydrogenation yield methylcyclohexane.

16.8.5.1.2 Addition of Halogens

Benzene reacts with chlorine or bromine in the presence of light to form benzene hexachloride and benzene hexabromide respectively. The reaction follow free radical addition mechanism.

It should be noted that the concept of resonance does not mean that these structures rapidly shifts between canonical forms. In fact, all the molecules of a substance have the same structure all the time, in which all the electrons are delocalized over the whole system involved in resonance.

Resonance Energy and Stability of Benzene

The resonance energy of a molecules is the difference between the energy of the most stable canonical form and that of the actual molecule. For benzene it can be calculated by measuring its heat of hydrogenation and comparing it with that of the most stable canonical from.

Hydrogenation of cyclohexene (having one double bond) evolves 120 kJ/mol heat energy to form cyclohexane.

Hydrogenation of cyclohexa–1,3–diene (having two double bonds) evolves 232 kJ/mol to form cyclohexane, which is almost double of the value 120 kJ/mol for cyclohexene.

The molecule cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene (Kekule structure) normally written for benzene and having three double bonds, should release energy three time to that of cyclohexane (i.e. 120×3 = 360 kJ/mol), upon hydrogenation.

But hydrogenation of benzene actually evolves only 208 kJ/mol.

Thus, the measured (experimental) heat of hydrogenation of benzene is less than the expected value of the most stable canonical form by an amount of 152 kJ/mol. Benzene is, therefore, is said to be resonance stabilized by an amount of 152 kJ/mol which is known as its resonance energy.

16.8.5 Reactivity and Reactions

Due to unusual stability (resonance stabilization), benzene and its derivatives do not give addition reactions like those of alkenes. In alkenes the pi electronic cloud is localized between the two carbon atoms and thus they readily undergo addition reactions. In benzene the pi electronic cloud makes a continuous sheet above and below all the six nuclei and the pi electrons are, thus delocalized, which give benzene more stability. Benzene, therefore, prefers to undergo electrophilic substitution reactions rather than addition reactions, to retain its aromatic character.

16.8.5.1 Addition Reactions

Benzene is very resistant to addition reaction and requires much more vigorous conditions than generally required for alkenes and alkynes. It does not undergo electrophilic addition reaction, but may give free-radical type addition and catalytic addition reactions in proper conditions.

16.8.5.1.1 Addition of Hydrogen

Benzene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of Ni, Pt or Pd catalyst at elevated temperature and high pressure to form cyclohexane. The reaction is also called catalytic hydrogenation.

Similarly toluene (a benzene derivative) upon catalytic hydrogenation yield methylcyclohexane.

16.8.5.1.2 Addition of Halogens

Benzene reacts with chlorine or bromine in the presence of light to form benzene hexachloride and benzene hexabromide respectively. The reaction follow free radical addition mechanism.
